sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: park versus drive, steering method by speed, hand positions, one-hand use and looking back while reversing
Confusable pairs among start-up and pull-away steps, the three steering methods, their hand positions and the backing procedure, followed by continuation facts; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec06-R01 | anchor: A01
The gear selector should be in park when you start the engine, and you move it to D for drive only when you are ready to pull away. [A01]
Why it matters: group starting; confusable park versus drive.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-R02 | anchor: A01
Stopping begins with a mirror check for traffic behind you, and only then does your foot move from the accelerator to the brake. [A01]
Why it matters: group stopping; difficulty medium.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0053]

FACT_ID: sec06-R03 | anchor: A02
The hand signals that may take one hand off the wheel are those for turning, slowing or stopping. [A02]
Why it matters: group hand position; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec06-R04 | anchor: A03
In push/pull steering your arms stay next to your body, which makes it more natural to keep both hands on the wheel the whole time. [A03]
Why it matters: group steering methods; difficulty low.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-R05 | anchor: A04
Hand-over-hand steering is for low-speed turns such as at intersections or when parking, while push/pull is the preferred method for normal driving. [A04]
Why it matters: group steering methods; confusable hand-over-hand versus push/pull.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-R06 | anchor: A04
While one hand reaches for a control, the hand that stays on the wheel keeps the normal operating position of 8 to 9 or 3 to 4 o'clock, the same areas where hand-over-hand steering starts. [A04]
Why it matters: group hand position; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-R07 | anchor: A04
Keeping one hand on the wheel at all times matters for vehicle balance, for handling steering reversals and for avoiding injury. [A04]
Why it matters: group one-hand steering; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-R08 | anchor: A05
Backing up is the only situation in which the manual recommends the 12 o'clock position, and its backing steps put the left hand there. [A05]
Why it matters: group backing; confusable twelve o'clock versus normal grip.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec06-R09 | anchor: A05
When reversing, your main view comes from turning to look through the rear window, while mirrors and a camera are only checked now and then. [A05]
Why it matters: group backing; confusable looking back versus relying on mirrors.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec06-R10 | anchor: A06
When backing you steer slightly toward where the rear should go, and your rearward look continues until the vehicle has fully stopped. [A06]
Why it matters: group backing; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0058]

corpus_stability.reason: The South Carolina Driver's Manual prints a single edition line (Revised 06/2024) on its front cover; its disclaimer says legislative and SCDMV policy changes may make some content out of date until the agency incorporates them, and a possibly newer unlinked upload exists on the issuer site (freshness debt in the run jams), so the corpus is treated as revised at most about once a year, bound to the registered snapshot.
